key_insight: Reducing measurable cognitive biases in LLMs does not automatically produce better decision-making; some biases are context-specific heuristics that can be functionally adaptive and improve outcomes in certain tasks.
problem_solved: Clarifies the mismatch between standard bias-reduction objectives and actual decision quality in LLMs, showing when removing biases may not yield better decisions and may even degrade performance in certain contexts.
method: Systematically measure a range of cognitive biases in multiple LLMs using established bias probes.
Evaluate decision-making performance of the same models across diverse tasks and contextual setups, comparing bias scores to outcome quality.
Analyze cases where biases correlate with improved or degraded decisions to identify when biases are functional versus harmful.
impact: Encourages practitioners to go beyond blanket bias removal and to assess mitigation techniques against real task outcomes and context — designing interventions that preserve useful heuristics or apply debiasing selectively.
visual_elements: Scatter plot: bias score (x) vs decision quality (y) showing weak or negative correlation and clusters where bias helps performance
Flowchart: evaluation pipeline from bias probes to decision-task outcomes to context-aware mitigation
Side-by-side examples: short prompt-response pairs where a biased heuristic yields a better vs worse decision
Icon set: bias (brain), decision quality (target), context (map), mitigation (shield) to summarize trade-offs
paper_title: LLMs displaying less cognitive bias are not necessarily better decision makers
paper_authors: Vittoria Dentella, Marco Marelli, Luca Rinaldi
